tools.description:
List iPhones connected over USB, to this Mac and to the account's other Macs

Only iPhones on a USB cable are listed; a phone near the Mac over Bluetooth or
Wi-Fi is not (macOS gives its screen only over USB). The iPhones are grouped by Mac,
always under a `mac <slug>:` header (`this Mac:` while signed out). Each line:
  <id>  <name>  <model> iOS <version>  <phone number>  [locked]  (bluetooth <state>, <pointer> pointer)
- id: stable on its Mac (same after rename, iOS update, cable replug). Pass it to `acquire -d`.
- Other Macs: while this Mac is signed in, list also shows the iPhones of every other
  online Mac of the account. `acquire -d <id>` takes one on its Mac and prints a lease
  like studio:42; every command then works from here. `daemon status` shows this
  Mac's slug. A Mac that does not answer is a warning; a Mac without iPhones is not listed.
- phone number: read from the SIM over USB. Missing without a SIM, but also when the
  carrier did not write it to the SIM: check `ghosthand info` for the SIM state.
- [locked]: unlock with `ghosthand unlock` before screenshots or input.
- [AssistiveTouch off]: no pointer on the phone. acquire turns it on.
- bluetooth connected: input works.
- bluetooth disconnected: paired; the Mac reconnects it in about 2 s. If it stays so,
  Bluetooth is off on the iPhone or it is out of range: tell the user to turn it on.
- bluetooth not paired: the next input command waits while the user pairs the Mac
  from iPhone Settings > Bluetooth (tap the Mac's name, then Pair).
- pointer: absolute, or relative when the first tap proved absolute does not move
  the pointer (seen on iOS 15 over BLE). Shown after the first tap.
- (xctest <state>) instead of bluetooth: the iPhone uses XCTest mode (`control --help`).
  stopped: the next command starts the runner (about 15 s); failed: see `control -l <id>`.
- Names do not matter: each screen is matched to its USB iPhone once and saved.
  Only several new iPhones with one name, plugged in together, cannot be matched:
  list warns. Plug them in one at a time once.
When no phone is found, the error says why per phone: not on USB, not trusted
(unlock it and tap Trust), or locked.
- Warning "macOS screen capture does not list it": a trusted iPhone was locked or
  untrusted when plugged in. Tell the user to replug its cable. Without a person,
  `ghosthand daemon restart` also fixes it (all screen capture stops for a few seconds).
- No iPhone listed, or one that is not trusted or paired: run `ghosthand setup` once.
  Tell the user to complete setup in the small Ghosthand window. Do not interact
  with it. Poll `ghosthand setup status` every 2 seconds until ready is true.
  Continue automatically; do not reopen setup or retry input.

Examples (arguments):
  {}

mac.description: Mac slug from list, e.g. "studio". Needed when several Macs are online

tools.name: list

tools.description:
Take exclusive use of an iPhone for a task. Prints a short lease id; pass it explicitly with -l to every other command

Every command that uses an iPhone (screenshot, screentext, tap, hold, swipe, key, mute,
unmute, type, unlock, lock, wake, record start, record stop, assistivetouch, rename, forget, control, random,
file, photo, app, info, logs, restart, shutdown) needs a lease and runs on its
iPhone; list and `random list` do not. -d picks the iPhone here only.
- Always pass --reason with the task you need the iPhone for. Other agents read it
  to decide if they wait or give up.
- stdout is only the lease ID with the Mac of the iPhone, e.g. studio:42 (`42` only
  while this Mac is signed out). Pass it exactly so on every device command.
  Tool-call environments may not persist. Do not rely on an exported lease.
- The ID works from every Mac of the account: for an iPhone on another Mac (see
  `list`), this Mac's daemon sends each command there through ghosthand.dev.
  Without -d, a Mac with no iPhone takes the account's only one.
- IDs increase in state.db and are never reused there. Do not delete or restore
  state.db: that resets the counter. --label is only display text, not proof of
  ownership; acquiring again with the same label does not resume an active lease.
- Lease numbers are not authentication. The tunnel needs an account token.
- The lease ends by itself after --idle-timeout seconds without a command, so a
  crashed agent never blocks the phone. Run `ghosthand release -l studio:42` when done.
- acquire turns AssistiveTouch on over USB (the pointer for tap and swipe) if it
  is off; release turns it off again.
- Busy: acquire fails at once and shows the label, its reason, when it was
  acquired and its last command. Read them, then decide: give up or tell the user
  the iPhone is busy, or run `ghosthand wait` to wait for it.
- Use --force only when that lease is stale (its holder is gone); the old holder's
  next command then fails. After --force, take a screenshot first.

CLI flags in this text are arguments: --reason = reason, --label = label, --idle-timeout = idleTimeoutSeconds, --device = device, --force = force

Examples (arguments):
  {"device":"7EF219AD-69B4-423E-B8C4-4F4A6140822F","label":"ses_123","reason":"reply to Anna in Messages"}

force.description: End another lease on the iPhone and take it

idleTimeoutSeconds.description: End the lease this long after its last call (default: 600)

label.description: Display text, e.g. your agent session id, shown to others

mac.description: Mac slug from list, e.g. "studio". Needed when several Macs are online

reason.description: Required. The task you need the iPhone for, e.g. "reply to Anna in Messages"

tools.description:
Wait until another lease on the iPhone ends, then acquire it. Use only after `acquire` said it is busy and you decided to wait

Prints the lease id like `acquire`. Retries every second (no queue order).
- Run `acquire` first and read who holds the iPhone and why. Wait only when your
  task can wait; otherwise give up or tell the user the iPhone is busy.
- On timeout it fails with the current lease's label and reason. Do not loop on wait.
- After wait, take a screenshot first: someone else used the phone.

tools.name: wait

tools.description:
End the lease from -l or GHOSTHAND_LEASE, so another client can acquire the iPhone

Waits for a running command of the lease to finish, then ends it.
- Turns AssistiveTouch off, also when it was on before acquire, so the person gets
  the phone back without a pointer. --keep-assistivetouch leaves it on.
- A lease that ends by its idle timeout turns it off too, a few seconds later.
- The output says "AssistiveTouch turned off" when it did. An iPhone not on USB
  is turned off later, when it is plugged in again with no lease.

tools.name: release

tools.description:
Save the current iPhone screen as PNG (or JPG) over USB, in about 0.3s

The image is in screen points (375x667 on an iPhone 6s, 414x896 on an XR): small
enough for LLM vision, and the same coordinates `tap` and `swipe` take.
- Prefer `screentext` when you only need text: no image to read.
- "No frame" means USB gave no fresh frame; it does not prove input failed.
  Check list and the display. If off and unlocked, use `wake -l <id>`; if on and
  unlocked, try daemon restart. Ask the user before restarting their iPhone.
- A locked iPhone gives no screenshot. Unlock only with a confirmed passcode.
  Never lock the phone to fix capture.
- Read the file only after the command returns. A read started in parallel with the
  capture can show the previous image.
- Password fields: screenshots often do not show the typed dots. An empty-looking
  secure field does not mean the password was not typed. Never type it again; check
  the result after you submit (next screen or error).
- Screen dimmed but no dialog in the image? Some system dialogs are hidden from USB
  capture (seen: App Store Install sheet, cellular data and location prompts).
  --native takes a real iOS screenshot (about 2 s): the dialog shows, at the
  same coordinates `tap` takes. It needs Bluetooth, an unlocked phone, and is deleted
  from Photos after reading. iOS shows a screenshot thumbnail at the bottom left for
  a few seconds; it does not block taps elsewhere.
- XCTest mode: the image comes from XCTest; hidden-dialog support is not verified.
  --native is not needed.

CLI flags in this text are arguments: --settle = settle, --native = native, --scale = scale

Examples (arguments):
  {"lease":"studio:42"}
  {"lease":"studio:42"}
  {"lease":"studio:42","native":true}

Read the text on the iPhone screen with on-device OCR. One line per text: `x,y wxh text` in screenshot coordinates (same space as tap)

Output: one line per text, `x,y wxh text`, top-left corner and size in screen
points. The center of a line is x+w/2, y+h/2. To tap text, use
`ghosthand tap --text "..."`, which does this for you.
Add --language for non-English UIs (it-IT, de-DE, ...) or accents are misread.

(Mail "6"), icons (read as stray letters like "Q", "A", "4"), text cut by
an edge. Text inside photos comes out garbled. Use a screenshot for these.

tools.name: screentext

tools.description:
Tap at screenshot coordinates or on text found by OCR, via the AssistiveTouch mouse pointer

Rules:
- Send the numbers you read in the screenshot; do not scale them.
- Home Screen app labels do not open apps: tap the icon, ~40 points above the label.
- --text: an exact line match wins over "contains"; several matches fail with a list,
  pick one with --index. OCR resolves the target once, before input.
- The AssistiveTouch floating button can cover what you tap; hide it
  (Settings > Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch > Always Show Menu off).
- App Store can show Resume while downloading. Check download/installation state
  before repeating taps; an unchanged label does not prove the click failed.
- Each press lasts 220...260 ms. Double taps have a 100...150 ms release-to-press gap,
  with no pointer movement between clicks. Use double-tap to select a word or zoom
  supported content, triple-tap to select a paragraph; app behavior varies. It is
  not a VoiceOver gesture or a side-button purchase confirmation.
- Long press (context menus, previews): `ghosthand hold`. Move an item after a long
  press: `ghosthand hold-drag`.
First use: pair the Mac from iPhone Settings > Bluetooth (tap the Mac's name, then
Pair); the command waits for it. Each tap turns AssistiveTouch on over USB if off.
A paired iPhone reconnects in about 2 s after a daemon start.
- Approaches accelerate then slow at the target. Timing varies; tap coordinates do not.
- The first pointer input of a lease moves the pointer to 2 spots first (+0.4 s, no
  click): iOS turns the pointer 90° from the screen when the iPhone lies on its side,
  and input is turned to match ("iOS pointer space is turned"). Do not turn the
  iPhone during a lease; if you must, acquire a new lease.
- Relative pointer (older iOS, only if absolute failed): after a daemon start, a reconnect or 60 s idle, the
  pointer first jumps to the top-left corner (+0.3 s). That is normal.

CLI flags in this text are arguments: --text = text, --index = index, --language = language, --screenshot = screenshot, --screentext = screentext, --scale = scale, --wait-text = waitText, --timeout-ms = timeoutMs

Examples (arguments):
  {"lease":"studio:42","screenshot":true,"x":207,"y":448}
  {"lease":"studio:42","screentext":true,"text":"General"}

language.description: OCR language, e.g. it-IT; en-US is always included

tools.description:
Press and hold (long press) at screenshot coordinates or on text found by OCR, via the AssistiveTouch mouse pointer

The button goes down, stays still for --duration, then goes up. Same targets as tap
(coordinates, or --text with --index).

  the icon, not its label. Close a menu with `key esc`.

- A button that ignored `tap`: read the screen, then press it once more (tap or
  `hold --duration 400`). A just-opened alert can ignore the first press; the second
  worked in the iOS 18 alert tests, with tap, hold or swipe alike.
- Still blocked: try `hold --duration 5000` at verified coordinates, then check the
  result. On an SE2, iOS 26.5.2, Apple Account's Do Not Sign Out accepted this after
  taps and 1500...2500 ms holds failed. One success; duration is not a proven cause.
- To move the item after the long press (reorder icons or rows), use `hold-drag`.

tools.name: hold

tools.description:
Swipe a finger like a person from (x1,y1) to (x2,y2) in screenshot coordinates: fast, lifted while moving. For TikTok, feeds, lists, carousels, Home Screen pages

The start point and the length (the distance to the end point) are yours; speed, easing
and a slight sideways bow are random on every call, so no two swipes are alike. Vary the
start and the length between calls: the same swipe every time is not human.
- Fast start, and the finger lifts while still moving, so lists keep scrolling
  (momentum). Content moves further than the swipe length. For an exact distance use
  `scroll`, or --duration 400 and more, which is slower but still lifts moving.
- TikTok: `swipe 200 700 200 250` swipes up from the lower middle: the next video.
  Both points must be on screen.
- Home Screen pages: start in empty space or on an app icon, not on a widget and not
  on the AssistiveTouch button.
- XCTest mode is fastest. Bluetooth mode needs ~100 ms more for the pointer to reach
  the start point; its first swipe after a connection measures the pointer speed (~1 s,
  one log line, the screen should be still).
- Items that need a long press first (Home Screen icons) use `hold-drag`; so does exact
  drag and drop.
Do not use it to go Home: `ghosthand key home`.

tools.description:
Scroll with the Bluetooth mouse wheel over a point (default: screen center). Use this to scroll web pages and lists; one tick is about 100 points

down shows content further down (like a finger swipe up); up shows content above.
right shows content further right (carousels, wide tables); left goes back.
- One tick moves about 100 points in Safari, about 115 in Settings-style lists
  (UITableView), measured on an XR (896 points high, so `scroll down 8` is about
  one screen). These are estimates: check the result with --screentext.

tools.description:
Start recording the iPhone screen and sound to a new .mov or .mp4 file. Stops by itself after 5 minutes; stop earlier with record stop

Returns at once; the recording runs in the daemon while you send input. Use any
other command meanwhile: screenshots, screentext and taps keep working.
- Local CLI and Unix-socket HTTP: the file is written on this Mac. The CLI makes a
  relative path absolute against its own folder. The folder must exist and the file
  must not: a recording never overwrites a file. Remote HTTP cannot choose a Mac path.
- MCP: omit path. The daemon owns a temporary file; record-stop returns an embedded
  resource blob up to 16 MiB, or a 1-day upload link up to 100 MB. Larger files need
  local collection on the Mac. Upload failures keep the recording for another record-stop
  while the lease is active. Delivery, a new recording or lease end removes temporary files.
- It stops by itself, and the file is complete, after --max-duration, when the
  lease ends (release, idle timeout, --force), or when the daemon stops. Run
  `record stop` to get its size and duration.
- The lease idle timeout still counts: send a command at least every 10 minutes
  (or acquire with a longer --idle-timeout), or the lease ends and so does the recording.
- One recording per iPhone at a time. A locked iPhone cannot start one.
- Video is H.264 at the native screen size (828x1792 on an XR); sound is AAC.
  Size measured on an XR: 3-5 MB per minute on a still screen, at most about
  17 MB per minute while the screen moves. --fps 30 lowers both.
- A dark display sends no frames: start fails with `no-frame`. Run `wake` first.
- The sound track is the iPhone's sound output. It is silent when nothing plays.
- With sound, record start and record stop pause media that is playing on the
  iPhone (iOS audio route change; tested on iOS 18.7). Start the recording first,
  then start playback; or press play again after record start. --no-audio does not pause it.
- The round AssistiveTouch button is in the video unless "Always Show Menu" is off
  (Settings > Accessibility > Touch > AssistiveTouch). USB cannot change that
  setting; ask the user before you change it in Settings. The mouse pointer dot stays in the video.

tools.description:
Open the setup window: connect a new iPhone over USB and Bluetooth, step by step

For a person, not an agent: shows Sign in with Google first (once per Mac), then
permissions (Allow Camera and Allow Bluetooth buttons), then one step at a time (plug
in, trust, unlock, pair over Bluetooth) and updates by itself every second. The Mac is discoverable over
Bluetooth only while this window shows the pairing step. When the iPhone is ready it
offers a prompt to copy for an agent.
- Agents: run this when the user wants to connect a new iPhone, or when `list` or an
  error shows no iPhone, an untrusted one, or a Bluetooth link that never connects.
  A locked iPhone that is trusted and paired needs `unlock` or the user, not setup.
  Tell the user to complete setup in the small Ghosthand window. All window actions
  are user-only; do not interact with it. Poll `ghosthand setup status` every 2 seconds until
  ready is true. Continue automatically. Do not retry input or reopen setup while waiting.
- Do not open it when an iPhone already works, or twice in a row.
- The daemon runs as Ghosthand.app, so permissions belong to Ghosthand, not your
  editor. Normal commands never show permission dialogs or open System Settings.
  Only user clicks in setup request permissions or open settings.
- The first setup adds the daemon to Login Items (LaunchAgent
  ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.remorses.ghosthand.daemon.plist), so it starts at login and
  after a crash. macOS may show a "Background Items Added" notification. A running
  daemon is kept. The user can turn it off in System Settings > General > Login Items;
  setup never turns it on again. Without it, commands still start the daemon on demand.
- In a sandboxed agent shell (Codex default), run setup with sandbox escalation: the
  sandbox blocks Launch Services. Never add --foreground: the app and daemon start
  outside the agent's process, so restarting the agent does not stop them.
- --permissions keeps the permissions checklist open even when access is already
  allowed. It never requests permission by itself.
Detaches at once, so the terminal is free and the window stays open after the
command exits. `dashboard` and `setup` share one process: running either again shows its
window. Starts the daemon when needed.
